USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay fully engaged in the active high-level negotiations and use the existing 10% tariff posture plus the March 1 deadline as leverage to lock in a substantive, enforceable deal — real structural reforms on IP and forced technology transfer, a credible purchase commitment, and a verification/enforcement mechanism. Do not escalate prematurely (a hike to 25% on $200B and threats of another $267B would hit US importers and fragile markets), but do not concede either: China has not yet tabled enforceable structural concessions.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading for the United States is a moderate opportunity, not a danger. Beijing is visibly overextended — GDP growth slowed to 6.6% in 2018 (lowest since 1990, Q4 at 6.4%) and December exports fell 4.4% y/y with imports from the US down 36% (Guardian/CNN/Diplomat). China has already moved first with concessions (resumed soybean purchases, cut auto tariffs), and US tariffs remain largely in place, giving Washington real leverage. The US economy is fundamentally resilient (industrial production roughly flat, CPI contained, unemployment low), so this sits near the -0.5 'leverage to extract concessions' anchor rather than -1.0. It is not a clean win because the US-China deficit actually widened to a record ~$345B despite a year of tariffs, and domestic fragility is real — the 10-year yield slid to 2.70%, consumer sentiment collapsed to 91.2, and the 35-day shutdown adds pressure on Trump to settle for optics. That is exactly why the action stance is negotiate-hold: keep pressing from strength without escalating into a March escalation that would raise costs for US firms (the bulk of Chinese imports are intermediate goods) and derail the fragile process, while refusing China's pattern of vague purchase promises in favor of enforceable structural commitments.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: We should stay inside the 90-day truce and keep negotiating with the US delegation now in Beijing (Jan 30-31) to prevent the reinstated 25% tariff on ~$200B of our exports and to protect Huawei. We should not escalate on the trade track in response to the Huawei charges — that would invite the very 25% step-up and faster US tech decoupling that would hurt us more. Hold our retaliation at the current level (Canadians detained as leverage) and pursue a deal that locks in the truce, contains the Huawei damage, and trades calibrated purchase commitments for a rollback of the threatened escalation.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high but not existential, anchoring at +0.5 on the CHN scale. Roughly $250B of our exports sit under US Section 301 tariffs, with the 25% hike on the ~$200B List 3 suspended for the 90-day window agreed at the G20 dinner (event_timeline 2018-12-01); losing that suspension is the main downside. Firm-level targeting of our flagship tech sector is real and escalating: Meng Wanzhou arrested Dec 1, DOJ unsealed fraud/sanctions charges and requested extradition Jan 28, and the US/UK/Aus/NZ have moved to block Huawei from 5G (web: theworld.org, BBC). The macro evidence confirms real economic bite: 2018 GDP hit a 28-year low, December exports fell 4.4% y/y (largest drop in two years) and imports -7.6%, the RMB depreciated ~6% in 2018 and equities fell ~20% (Reuters GDP instantview; CNBC Dec trade; World Bank China Update). That is material export-sector damage and FX pressure — consistent with the +0.5 anchor. But it is not existential: the 25% escalation is currently suspended and high-level talks (Lighthizer/Mnuchin in Beijing, Jan 30) are actively discussing purchase commitments while structural IP/tech-transfer issues remain open (event_timeline 2019-01-30), signaling the US wants a deal and giving us leverage. On action, the disciplined reading is that escalation now would make the situation worse — we are the party more exposed to a tariff step-up and technology decoupling, and the treaty path that could spare us (avoiding the 25% hike, containing Huawei) is open. High threat here argues for de-escalatory negotiation, not provocation. Hence negotiate at ~0.0: engage to lock in the truce and convert purchase-commitment discussions into a deal, without new unilateral concessions on core structural issues.
